summary: Defines how SNMPv2 messages are carried over an initial set of transport protocols. It was replaced by RFC 3417.

subtitle: Defines how SNMPv2 management messages are carried over various network transports.

tldr.problem: SNMPv2 management messages needed to be carried over multiple transport protocols (not just IP), and the message serialization had to be standardized across these different transports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps SNMPv2 messages onto UDP, OSI (CLNS/CONS), AppleTalk DDP, and IPX, with well-known ports and sockets defined for each. Messages are serialized using Abstract Syntax Notation (ASN.1) and Basic Encoding Rules (BER).
tldr.outcome: While these mappings allow SNMP to operate across diverse network architectures, UDP became the de facto standard. The RFC was replaced by RFC 3417, which consolidated and updated the transport definitions.

today: RFC 1906 defines the SNMPv2 transport mappings. It was obsoleted by RFC 3417, which consolidated the transport definitions with SNMPv3 and updated the specifications. UDP over IPv4 remains by far the most common transport for SNMP in practice, though IPX is largely obsolete and OSI is rarely deployed for SNMP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1906 specifies how SNMPv2 (version 2 of the Simple Network Management Protocol) messages can be transported over an initial set of network protocols. A management system consists of management stations (applications that monitor and control networks), agents (software on managed devices like routers and servers), and the protocol that carries messages between them. This RFC defines the transport layer mappings—the ways SNMP can be carried over different underlying networks.

The RFC establishes that UDP is the preferred mapping for greatest interoperability. However, it also defines optional mappings over OSI (CLNS and CONS), AppleTalk DDP, and IPX to support diverse network environments. Each mapping specifies serialization rules, well-known ports or sockets, and minimum message sizes that implementations must support.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a way to manage network devices. This RFC tells you how to send SNMP messages over different types of networks—the main way is UDP, but it also works over other networks if you need it.

sections.title: UDP and Transport Addresses
sections.content:
SNMPv2 over UDP is the preferred transport and should be the primary mapping in all implementations. UDP port 161 is the standard port for SNMP agents (devices being managed) to listen on, and port 162 is for notification sinks (trapd daemons) that receive unsolicited notifications from agents.

A SnmpUDPAddress is 6 octets: four octets for the IPv4 address (in network byte order) followed by two octets for the UDP port. Implementations must be able to accept SNMPv2 messages at least 484 octets in size, though larger sizes are encouraged. This minimum size accommodates typical management queries and bulk transfer requests without fragmentation.
sections.eli5: UDP uses numbered 'mailboxes' called ports. Management devices listen on port 161, and devices that receive alerts listen on port 162. Each message must fit in at least 484 bytes.

sections.title: Alternative Transports: OSI, DDP, and IPX
sections.content:
For organizations that use OSI networks, SNMPv2 can be carried over CLNS (Connectionless Network Service) or CONS (Connection-Oriented Network Service) using the OSI Transport Service. SnmpOSIAddress contains an NSAP (Network Service Access Point) of 3 to 20 octets followed by a TSEL (Transport Service Element) of up to 64 octets. Agents listen on transport selector 'snmp-l' (for connectionless) or 'snmp-o' (for connection-oriented), with traps on 'snmpt-l' and 'snmpt-o' respectively.

SNMPv2 over AppleTalk DDP uses DDP protocol type 8. Agents listen on DDP socket 8 and notification sinks on socket 9. Instead of numeric addresses, AppleTalk uses named services via NBP (Name Binding Protocol). SNMPv2 agents register with NBP type 'SNMP Agent', and traps use 'SNMP Trap Handler'. NBP names should be stable and stored in non-volatile storage. Since AppleTalk addresses can change dynamically, caching name-to-address mappings is recommended to minimize network traffic and protocol overhead.

SNMPv2 over IPX (Novell NetWare networks) uses IPX packet type 4 (Packet Exchange Protocol). Agents listen on IPX socket 36879 (0x900F hex) and notification sinks on socket 36880 (0x9010 hex). IPX deployments must support at least 546-octet messages.
sections.eli5: SNMP can also run over other networks: OSI networks use NSAPs and transport selectors, AppleTalk uses named services that can change, and IPX (Novell) uses numbered sockets like UDP.

sections.title: Serialization and ASN.1 Encoding
sections.content:
All SNMPv2 messages are serialized using Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) with Basic Encoding Rules (BER). The RFC specifies strict rules for BER encoding: the definite form (not indefinite form) must be used for lengths, primitive form for simple types and constructed form only for structured types, and specific handling of bit strings and octet strings.

Every SNMPv2 message consists of a version field, community string (for SNMPv2c) or security parameters (for SNMPv3), and a Protocol Data Unit (PDU) containing the actual management operation (GET, SET, GET-BULK, TRAP, etc.) and variable bindings (the data being queried or modified). The RFC includes an example of encoding a GetBulkRequest-PDU in hexadecimal, showing how ASN.1 types (INTEGER, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, SEQUENCE) map to encoded bytes.
sections.eli5: All SNMP messages are written in a standard format called ASN.1 BER. This is like a standard envelope format that works the same way no matter which postal service (UDP, AppleTalk, or IPX) carries the message.

sections.title: SNMPv1 Proxy Support
sections.content:
To support migration and coexistence, RFC 1906 defines a mechanism for SNMPv2 entities to proxy SNMPv1 (RFC 1157) messages. A proxy agent can receive SNMPv1 messages from legacy devices or management stations and translate them to SNMPv2 format (or vice versa), allowing SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 networks to interoperate. The RFC indicates that RFC 1908 ("Coexistence between Version 1 and Version 2") specifies the detailed behavior of such proxy agents.

The RFC recommends that implementations supporting alternative transports (OSI, DDP, IPX) also provide proxy service to the UDP mapping, ensuring maximum interoperability across heterogeneous network environments.
sections.eli5: Old SNMP version 1 devices can still talk to SNMPv2 devices through a translator, so you don't have to upgrade everything at once.
